You are a coding assistant that maintains and refactors the code in the
current project directory, like Claude Code. You act through tools: you do
not just describe changes, you make them.

Tools: list_directory, read_file (optionally start/end lines), grep,
insert_above (add lines above an existing line), edit_file (replace exact
existing text), write_file (new files),
for_each (same task over a list of items), run_command (shell; the user
approves it), ask_user.

How to work:
- Look before you change anything: read_file the file you will edit and
  any file whose contents you need to know. Never guess what code does -
  read it. Attached files in the user's message are already read.
- Change files with insert_above (adding lines, e.g. a comment above a
  function) or edit_file (replacing text), in small steps, one change per
  call, with anchor/old_string copied exactly from what you just read.

- A job that repeats over many things is ALWAYS a for_each call, never
  something you do yourself one by one: you only list the items and
  write the task once, for_each does the work. Example - "document every
  function in lib/foo.h from lib/foo/<name>.c": read lib/foo.h (if not
  attached), then call for_each(items=["foo_a", "foo_b", ...], task="In
  lib/foo.h add a 1-2 line comment above the declaration of {item}, based
  on what its source lib/foo/{item}.c does").
- Make only the change that was asked for. Keep the existing code and
  its style as it is: same indentation, same comment style as the
  neighbouring code, no reformatting, no renaming.
- If an edit_file call returns an error, read the file again and retry
  with corrected text.
- When finished, check with run_command (`git diff`, build, tests) if
  that is possible, then reply with a short summary of what you changed.
  Do not paste the whole file into your reply.
- Ask the user (ask_user) only if something genuinely cannot be found out
  by looking.

# qjs-lws

[libwebsockets](https://libwebsockets.org/) bindings for QuickJS.

Documentation site: [rsenn.github.io/qjs-lws](https://rsenn.github.io/qjs-lws/)

Build instructions: [`doc/building.md`](doc/building.md).
Full API reference: [`doc/`](doc/README.md).

```js
import { LWSContext } from 'lws';
```

## `LWSContext`

```js
const ctx = new LWSContext(info);
```

When `info.port` is set (i.e. the context listens), prefer the
equivalent `createServer(info)` — it's the same constructor call
under a name that reads better at a server call site:

```js
import { createServer } from 'lws';

const ctx = createServer(info);
```

`info` mirrors `struct lws_context_creation_info`. Recognised keys
(see [`doc/native/LWSContext.md`](doc/native/LWSContext.md) for the full list):

| Property | Type | Description |
|----------|------|-------------|
| `port`                 | number | TCP port to listen on (omit for a client-only context) |
| `vhostName`            | string | Virtual host name |
| `iface`                | string | Interface to bind |
| `options`              | number | OR-mask of `LWS_SERVER_OPTION_*` |
| `mounts`               | array  | HTTP mount points — see [`doc/native/mounts.md`](doc/native/mounts.md) |
| `protocols`            | array  | Protocol handler objects (below) |
| `listenAcceptRole`     | string | Role applied with `LWS_SERVER_OPTION_FALLBACK_TO_APPLY_LISTEN_ACCEPT_CONFIG` |
| `listenAcceptProtocol` | string | Protocol applied with the role |
| `serverSslCert` / `serverSslPrivateKey` / `serverSslCa` | string \| ArrayBuffer | TLS material — see [`doc/native/tls.md`](doc/native/tls.md) |

Property names accept both `camelCase` and `snake_case`.

### Protocol handler

Each entry of `protocols` maps to one `struct lws_protocols`. You
can implement either a single generic `callback` or named
`onEventName` handlers (mix as needed):

```js
{
  name: 'my-protocol',

  // Named handler — receives only the event-specific args.
  onEstablished(wsi)             { /* `this` is per-connection state */ },
  onReceive(wsi, data, len)      { wsi.write(data); },
  onClosed(wsi)                  { },

  // Generic fall-back. Receives the integer reason explicitly.
  callback(wsi, reason, ...args) { return 0; },
}
```

- `wsi` is an `LWSSocket` — see [`doc/native/LWSSocket.md`](doc/native/LWSSocket.md).
- The handler's `this` is a per-connection plain object the binding
  allocates automatically (libwebsockets `user` data); use it to
  carry connection-local state.
- The named handler is derived from the `LWS_CALLBACK_*` enum by
  camelCasing and prefixing with `on`:
  `LWS_CALLBACK_CLIENT_ESTABLISHED` → `onClientEstablished`.
  Lookup table is in `lws_callback_names[]` (`lws.c`); the
  conversion is exposed at runtime as `getCallbackName(n)` and
  `getCallbackNumber(name)`.

Common reason constants (exported on the module — `import {…} from 'lws'`):

| Constant | Value | When |
|----------|-------|------|
| `LWS_CALLBACK_ESTABLISHED`        |

# CLAUDE.md

Behavioral guidelines to reduce common LLM coding mistakes. Merge with project-specific instructions as needed.

**Tradeoff:** These guidelines bias toward caution over speed. For trivial tasks, use judgment.

## 1. Think Before Coding

**Don't assume. Don't hide confusion. Surface tradeoffs.**

Before implementing:
- State your assumptions explicitly. If uncertain, ask.
- If multiple interpretations exist, present them - don't pick silently.
- If a simpler approach exists, say so. Push back when warranted.
- If something is unclear, stop. Name what's confusing. Ask.

## 2. Simplicity First

**Minimum code that solves the problem. Nothing speculative.**

- No features beyond what was asked.
- No abstractions for single-use code.
- No "flexibility" or "configurability" that wasn't requested.
- No error handling for impossible scenarios.
- If you write 200 lines and it could be 50, rewrite it.

Ask yourself: "Would a senior engineer say this is overcomplicated?" If yes, simplify.

## 3. Surgical Changes

**Touch only what you must. Clean up only your own mess.**

When editing existing code:
- Don't "improve" adjacent code, comments, or formatting.
- Don't refactor things that aren't broken.
- Match existing style, even if you'd do it differently.
- If you notice unrelated dead code, mention it - don't delete it.

When your changes create orphans:
- Remove imports/variables/functions that YOUR changes made unused.
- Don't remove pre-existing dead code unless asked.

The test: Every changed line should trace directly to the user's request.

## 4. Goal-Driven Execution

**Define success criteria. Loop until verified.**

Transform tasks into verifiable goals:
- "Add validation" → "Write tests for invalid inputs, then make them pass"
- "Fix the bug" → "Write a test that reproduces it, then make it pass"
- "Refactor X" → "Ensure tests pass before and after"

For multi-step tasks, state a brief plan:
```
1. [Step] → verify: [check]
2. [Step] → verify: [check]
3. [Step] → verify: [check]
```

Strong success criteria let you loop independently. Weak criteria ("make it work") require constant clarification.

---

**These guidelines are working if:** fewer unnecessary changes in diffs, fewer rewrites due to overcomplication, and clarifying questions come before implementation rather than after mistakes.

## BUGS file format

Newly discovered bugs (see root `CLAUDE.md`, "Track Newly Discovered Bugs")
are appended to `BUGS` in this directory, one entry per bug, in the order
found, shaped like:

    - <canonical-name> (<file>:<line>): <short plain-text description
      of what's broken and how it was confirmed>

        <JS code that triggers it, or a one-line note if not
        practically reproducible in plain JS>

`canonical-name` is a short kebab-case handle for referring back to the
bug elsewhere (commit messages, other BUGS entries). The source location
is the primary place the bug lives, not every place it's felt.

message(STATUS "${PROJECT_NAME} ${PROJECT_VERSION}")

# A musl toolchain must not pick up the host's (glibc) libraries and headers:
# search for dependencies only below CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH, and have pkg-config
# look only there too. Whatever isn't found there gets built from source.
option(FIND_ONLY_IN_PREFIX "Only search CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH for libraries, headers and packages" OFF)
if(CMAKE_C_COMPILER MATCHES "musl" OR FIND_ONLY_IN_PREFIX)
  if(CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH)
    list(APPEND CMAKE_FIND_ROOT_PATH ${CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH})
    set(CMAKE_FIND_ROOT_PATH_MODE_LIBRARY ONLY)
    set(CMAKE_FIND_ROOT_PATH_MODE_INCLUDE ONLY)
    set(CMAKE_FIND_ROOT_PATH_MODE_PACKAGE ONLY)

    set(_pc_dirs "")
    foreach(_prefix ${CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH})
      file(GLOB _multiarch RELATIVE "${_prefix}/lib" "${_prefix}/lib/*-linux-*")
      list(APPEND _pc_dirs "${_prefix}/lib/pkgconfig" "${_prefix}/share/pkgconfig")
      foreach(_dir ${_multiarch})
        list(APPEND _pc_dirs "${_prefix}/lib/${_dir}/pkgconfig")
      endforeach(_dir)
    endforeach(_prefix)
    string(REPLACE ";" ":" _pc_dirs "${_pc_dirs}")
    set(ENV{PKG_CONFIG_LIBDIR} "${_pc_dirs}")
    message(STATUS "Searching only in: ${CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH}")
  else(CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH)
    message(WARNING "FIND_ONLY_IN_PREFIX/musl: CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH is empty, searching the system as usual")
  endif(CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH)
endif()

```markdown
# chat-bridge

`chat-bridge.js` drives a chatbot **web page in a real browser** over the
Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP) and exposes it either on the command line or
as an **OpenAI-compatible HTTP endpoint**. Any OpenAI client, ollama-repl
included, can then use the free web tiers of DeepSeek, Qwen, Gemini, Kimi,
ChatGPT, Duck.ai, DeepAI, OpenRouter and Mistral as if they were an API.

It exists because those sites have no (free) API, only a chat page that is
logged in once in a browser. The bridge types into that page and reads the
answer back out of the DOM.

- [Usage](#usage)
- [Design](#design)
- [Specification](#specification)
- [Sites](#sites)
- [Install](#install)
- [Limits](#limits)
- [Backlog](#backlog)

Files: `chat-bridge.js` (the program), `README.md` (this document),
`PROVIDERS.md` (what each site can do, quirks, billing), `TODO.md` (open work).

## Usage

    qjsm chat-bridge.js [options] serve            OpenAI-style server
    qjsm chat-bridge.js [options] send "prompt"    type, submit, print
    qjsm chat-bridge.js [options] read             print latest reply
    qjsm chat-bridge.js [options] eval "expr"      raw Runtime.evaluate
    qjsm chat-bridge.js list                       list page tabs

| option | default | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `--site NAME` | first open | site for `send`/`read`/`eval` |
| `--port N` | 9222 | browser CDP port |
| `--host H` | 127.0.0.1 | browser CDP host |
| `--listen N` | 8089 | `serve`: HTTP port, 0 = any free port (the startup line prints the real one) |
| `--max N` | 3 | `serve`: chat tabs per site |
| `--allow-paid` | off | `serve`: also use pay-as-you-go sites (`billing: 'metered'`, now openrouter); also `CHAT_BRIDGE_ALLOW_PAID=1` |
| `--idle SEC` | 2.5 | reply unchanged this long = finished |
| `--timeout SEC` | 180 | give up waiting for a reply |

Prerequisite: a browser with a dedicated profile, logged in once to the
sites you want, started with remote debugging:

    google-chrome --remote-debugging-port=9222 \
      --user-data-dir=$HOME/.chat-bridge-profile \
      https://chat.deepseek.com https://chat.qwen.ai

From ollama-repl, which can start the bridge itself:

    qjsm ../ollama-repl/repl.js --provider bridge

That runs `serve` on a free port, picks one of the available models in turn
(or use `--model NAME`), fails over to another when one hits its limit (after
compacting the conversation, see below), and stops the bridge on exit. `--cdp-host`/`--cdp-port` name the browser. Or run
the bridge yourself:

    qjsm chat-bridge.js serve
    OPENAI_API_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8089/v1 OPENAI_API_KEY=x \
      qjsm ../ollama-repl/repl.js --provider openai --model deepseek

`serve` checks the browser first and exits with the command to start one if
nothing answers on the CDP port.

The **model name selects the site** (`deepseek`, `qwen`, ...): the first
site whose name the model string contains.

## Design

### Principles

- **Real browser, real session.** No scraping of private endpoints, no
  credentials handled: the browser already holds the login.
- **Loopback only.** The endpoint types into logged-in sessions, so `serve`
  binds `127.0.0.1` and has no authentication.
- **Never steal focus.** Tabs the bridge opens are background tabs, text is
  entered with `Input.insertText` and submitted with a real Enter key event
  dispatched over CDP; the user's own tabs and keyboard focus are left alone.
- **Own your tabs.** `serve` opens up to `--max` tabs per site and closes
  them again on SIGINT/SIGTERM. A tab is closed earlier only when it is of no
  use any more: its site hit a message limit, so it cannot receive a prompt
  until the limit resets. A chat that was used and can still take a prompt is
  never closed, and neither is a tab waiting for you to log in or accept a
  dialog. It never reuses or closes tabs it did not
  create (`send`/`read`/`eval` are the exception: they attach to an
  existing tab of the site).

### Components

| piece | role |
|---|---|
| `CDP` | one WebSocket to a tab or to the browser, request/response by `id`, `eval()` helper over `Runtime.evaluate` |
| `SITES` / `ACTIVE` | per-site table (host, home URL, input selector, reply selector); `ACTIVE` is `SITES` without entries that carry a `skip` reason |
| `Chat` | one browser tab: its CDP session, the `history` it is known to hold, `busy` flag, a promise chain that serializes asks |
| `Bridge` | the tab pool per site, tab discovery over `/json`, `acquire()`/`release()` |
| `planPrompt()` | decides between "send only the new turn" and "replay the transcript" |
| `toolPreamble()` / `extractCalls()` | tool calling emulation |
| `completions()` | the `/v1/chat/completions` handler |

### Request flow

    client ──POST /v1/chat/completions──▶ completions()
        pick site from `model`
        Bridge.acquire(site, messages)   ── tab holding this history,
                                            else an idle tab,
                                            else a new tab (≤ --max),
                                            else wait for a release
        planPrompt()                     ── continue or fresh
        Chat.ask(prompt)                 ── type, Enter, poll the DOM
        ◀── JSON or SSE ──
        Bridge.release()

### Context handling

OpenAI clients send the **whole message history with every request**. The
bridge keeps, per tab, the exact message list the open chat holds
(`chat.history`, including the assistant reply it just produced).

- **Continuation:** if the request minus its last user turn equals a free
  tab's history, line for line, the request goes to that tab and only the new
  user turn is typed. The site's own conversation carries on.
- **New context:** otherwise an idle tab is reset (`newChat()` navigates to
  the site's home page, only if the tab is dirty) and the entire transcript is
  flattened into one prompt (`System: … User: … Assistant:`).
- A new context therefore needs no signal from the client: `/clear`, an edited
  or rewound history, a different conversation, all simply fail to match.
- After an error the tab's history is cleared, so the next request replays
  the transcript instead of trusting a half-sent state.

### Reply detection

The reply text is read by querying the site's `reply` selector and taking the
**last** match. A reply is *new* when the match count grew or its text
differs from before the send. It is *finished* when the text stayed unchanged
for `--idle` seconds. There is no portable "generation done" signal across
sites, hence the idle timer.

### Streaming

`stream: true` yields an SSE chunk each time the reply text grows, but only
for **append-only** growth. A rewrite of earlier text (some sites re-render
markdown) waits until the text is append-only again.

### Tool calling (emulated)

Web chats have no tool API. For a request with `tools`:

1. On a fresh chat the first prompt is prefixed with `toolPreamble()`: the
   tools are described, a worked example call is shown, and the model is told
   to answer a call with only a fenced `tool_call` JSON block. Later requests
   to the same chat get a short reminder (`TOOL_REMINDER`) appended instead.
2. Tool results come back as `role: tool` messages and are flattened to
   `[tool result]` lines; earlier assistant tool calls are re-rendered as the
   same fenced blocks, so the model sees a consistent transcript.
3. The reply is scanned by `extractCalls()` for top-level
   `{"name":…, "arguments":…}` objects whose name is a declared tool, however
   the page decorated them. Matches become `tool_calls` and
   `finish_reason: "tool_calls"`.
4. Calls can only be told apart once the reply is complete, so a request
   **with tools is answered whole even when streaming was asked**.

Measured per site (PROVIDERS.md): deepseek, qwen, gemini, kimi and mistral
follow the protocol and passed a coding task; chatgpt (logged out), duck and
deepai still ignore it, even with the worked example (duck sometimes obeys
with the end-of-prompt reminder).

### Refusals

While waiting for a reply the bridge also watches the page. It reports, as
OpenAI-style errors with a `Retry-After` header where a time is known:

| situation | status / `error.code` | how it is detected |
|---|---|---|
| quota or rate limit used up | 429 `rate_limit_exceeded` | new page text (not there before the send, not part of the prompt) matches `LIMIT_RE`; reset time parsed from "in 3 Stunden" style text, else 15 min |
| login wanted | 401 `login_required` | the tab moved to a login/auth path |
| prompt never taken | 502 `prompt_not_accepted` | the input did not empty after four Enter presses |

The unsent prompt is cleared from the input box. A site that refused is put
on **cooldown** for the `Retry-After` time: later requests for it fail at
once, without touching the browser. For `stream: true` the status is
returned before any chunk, so a client sees a real HTTP error.
ollama-repl uses this to fail over to another model.

### Billing guard

Nothing the bridge does can buy anything: it types into the prompt box and
presses Enter. Still, three guards keep it that way.

- **`billing` class per site.** `free` (the default) is a consumer chat that
  costs money only if a human clicks Upgrade. `metered` is pay-as-you-go
  credits or an API-style account (openrouter; aistudio and groq, if they
  were adopted). A metered site is **refused unless the bridge runs with
  `--allow-paid`**: requests get HTTP 402 `paid_site_blocked`, and `/v1/models`
  lists it with `available: false, unavailable: "billing_guard"`, so
  ollama-repl's rotation and failover skip it on their own.
- **Enter only in the prompt box.** Before each Enter the bridge focuses the
  prompt box and checks that it holds the focus; otherwise Enter could
  activate a stray button (an Upgrade dialog). No focus, no Enter
  (`prompt_not_accepted`).
- **Payment pages.** If a send makes the tab move to a checkout, billing,
  pricing, subscribe, upgrade, payment, purchase or plans path, the request
  fails with 402 `payment_page_reached` and the site cools down for 5 minutes.

## Specification

### HTTP endpoints

| method, path | behaviour |
|---|---|
| `GET /v1/models` | one entry per active site, `owned_by: "chat-bridge"`, plus `available` (false while on cooldown) and, then, `unavailable` (kind) and `resets_at` |
| `POST /v1/chat/completions` | OpenAI chat completion; `messages`, `model`, `stream`, `tools` are honoured |

Everything else returns 404. Fields that are accepted and ignored:
`temperature`, `max_tokens`, `stop`, `top_p`, `response_format`, … (a web
chat offers no such knobs). `usage` is always zero.

Errors: bad JSON → 400, no messages → 400, tab/site problems → 502, no reply
before `--timeout` → 504, site refusals as in [Refusals](#refusals).

### Site table entry

    name: {
      host,   // hostname of the chat page, used to match open tabs
      home,   // URL that opens a fresh chat
      input,  // selector of the prompt box (first visible match)
      reply,  // selector of the assistant messages (last match is read)
      billing, // 'free' (default) or 'metered', see Billing guard
      skip,   // optional: why the site was looked at and not adopted
    }

`input` is waited for (up to 20 s) before typing; "input field not found,
selector outdated?" means the site changed its markup. An input that has
emptied again is how the bridge knows the page took the prompt: Enter is
repeated up to four times until it does.

### Concurrency

One prompt at a time per tab (a promise chain per `Chat`); parallel requests
use parallel tabs up to `--max` per site, extra requests wait for a release.

## Sites

Status as of 2026-11. "verified" = a prompt/reply round trip through `serve`.

| site | status | notes |
|---|---|---|
| deepseek | verified | plain, streaming, tool calls |
| qwen | verified | plain, streaming, tool calls |
| gemini | verified | plain, streaming, tool calls (a replayed transcript is read as instructions) |
| kimi | verified | plain, streaming, tool calls; EU users: `www.kimi.ai/chat` (not `kimi.com`) |
| chatgpt | verified, logged out layout | logged-in layout not tested; input `#prompt-textarea, #mobile-composer-prompt, div.ProseMirror`; chat only, ignores tools |
| duck | verified (chat only) | needs the terms dialog accepted once by the user; ignores tools |
| deepai | verified (chat only) | ignores tools; can sit in an image-edit mode |
| openrouter | verified, **metered** | pay-as-you-go: refused unless `--allow-paid`; very slow stream |
| mistral | verified (plain, multi-turn, streaming, tools) | free tier has a message limit; concurrency and a long stream untested because the limit was hit |
| venice | skipped | no reply read in a test (anonymous use is rate-limited and gated) |
| aistudio | skipped | free Gemini API key exists, and gemini is already covered |
| groq | skipped | API playground behind a login, not a chat; groq has an OpenAI-compatible API |

`mistral.ai/products/vibe` was also considered: it is a product page for a
coding CLI, not a chat, so it has no entry.

To add a site: open it logged in, find the prompt box and the element that
holds one assistant reply (`eval` is made for this), add a `SITES` entry,
then check plain, multi-turn, streaming and a tool request through `serve`.
Prefer stable attributes (`data-*`, utility classes) over hashed class names.

## Install

`cmake --install` puts it in `bin/` as `chat-bridge`. The build copies
`examples/chat-bridge.js` with the in-repo `../lib/` import prefix stripped
(`cmake/subst-lib-imports.cmake`), so the imports resolve as bare module
names from the QuickJS module dir.

## Limits

- Needs a running, logged-in browser; sites change their markup without
  notice, so selectors rot.
- Free tiers have their own message limits, captchas, consent dialogs and
  terms pages. The bridge does not click through any of them on purpose.
- Replay of a long transcript into a fresh chat is one big text prompt: it
  costs the site's context and quota.
- Context matching is exact; a client that rewrites old messages
  (compaction, edited system prompt) triggers a replay every time.
- No token accounting, no sampling parameters.
- Use only with accounts and services whose terms allow automated use.

## Backlog

Open work is tracked in [TODO.md](TODO.md); bugs in `BUGS` at the repo root.
```

Key technical details include:

Mechanism: It uses CDP to insert text and dispatch Enter key events in background tabs.
Context Handling: It matches request history against tab history to decide whether to continue a conversation or replay the whole transcript into a new chat.

Concurrency: It manages a pool of tabs (up to --max per site) to handle parallel requests.
